questions.question: Let $*$ be the binary operation on $N$ defined by $a*b=\mathrm{L.C.M.}$ of $a$ and $b$. Find the value of $5*7$.
questions.answer:
The operation returns the **least common multiple** of the two numbers.

$$5*7=\mathrm{LCM}(5,7)$$

Both $5$ and $7$ are prime and neither divides the other, so their LCM is simply their product:

$$\therefore\ 5*7=5\times7=35$$

**The value is 35.**

(Note this is also $5\times7$ because $5$ and $7$ are coprime; for instance $4*6=\mathrm{LCM}(4,6)=12\ne24$, so $*$ is *not* ordinary multiplication.)

questions.question: Find the principal value of $\mathrm{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)$.
questions.answer:
The principal branch of $\mathrm{cosec}^{-1}$ takes values in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\setminus\{0\}$.

Let $\mathrm{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)=\alpha$. Then

$$\mathrm{cosec}\,\alpha=-\sqrt2\ \Rightarrow\ \sin\alpha=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$

The angle in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ with $\sin\alpha=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ is

$$\alpha=-\frac{\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ \mathrm{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)=-\frac{\pi}{4}$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet first writes $\mathrm{cosec}\,\alpha=-\sqrt2=\mathrm{cosec}\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$ and hence $\alpha=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, then correctly observes that $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ lies outside the principal range $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and amends it to $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. The final answer $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is correct (the intermediate $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ is a general solution, not the principal one).

questions.question: Construct a $(2\times2)$ matrix $A=[a_{ij}]$ whose elements are given by $a_{ij}=\dfrac{i}{j}$.
questions.answer:
A $2\times2$ matrix is

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{bmatrix},\qquad a_{ij}=\frac{i}{j}$$

Compute each entry:

$$a_{11}=\frac{1}{1}=1,\qquad a_{12}=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$a_{21}=\frac{2}{1}=2,\qquad a_{22}=\frac{2}{2}=1$$

$$\therefore\ A=\begin{bmatrix}1&\frac12\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}$$

The diagonal entries are all $1$ (since $a_{ii}=\frac ii=1$), and $a_{ij}\cdot a_{ji}=1$ for every pair — each off-diagonal entry is the reciprocal of its mirror image.

questions.question: Find the value(s) of $x$: $\begin{vmatrix}x&2\\ 18&x\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\ 18&6\end{vmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
Evaluate both determinants with $\begin{vmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc$:

$$\begin{vmatrix}x&2\\ 18&x\end{vmatrix}=x\cdot x-2\cdot18=x^{2}-36$$

$$\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\ 18&6\end{vmatrix}=6\cdot6-2\cdot18=36-36=0$$

Equating:

$$x^{2}-36=0\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}=36$$

$$\therefore\ x=\pm6$$

**Both roots are solutions: $x=6$ and $x=-6$.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet gives only $x=6$. The equation is quadratic in $x$, so $x=-6$ also satisfies it ($(-6)^{2}-36=0$ ✓) and must be included.

questions.question: Find the slope of tangent to the curve $y=3x^{3}-4x$ at $x=4$.
questions.answer:
The slope of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the given point. Differentiating:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=9x^{2}-4$$

At $x=4$:

$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=4}=9(4)^{2}-4=9(16)-4$$

$$=144-4=140$$

$$\therefore\ \text{slope}=140$$

(The point of contact is $(4,\,3(64)-16)=(4,176)$.)

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$: $y=\sin x^{2}$.
questions.answer:
Here the sine is taken of $x^{2}$ (not $(\sin x)^2$), so put $t=x^{2}$:

$$y=\sin t,\qquad t=x^{2}$$

$$\frac{dy}{dt}=\cos t,\qquad \frac{dt}{dx}=2x$$

By the chain rule,

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{dt}\cdot\frac{dt}{dx}=\cos t\cdot2x$$

Substituting back $t=x^{2}$:

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2x\cos x^{2}$$

*(Contrast with $y=\sin^{2}x$, whose derivative is $2\sin x\cos x=\sin2x$.)*

questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int\tan x\cdot\sec^{2}x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Put $t=\tan x$, so that

$$dt=\sec^{2}x\,dx$$

The integrand becomes $t\,dt$:

$$\int\tan x\sec^{2}x\,dx=\int t\,dt=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C$$

$$\therefore\ \int\tan x\sec^{2}x\,dx=\frac{\tan^{2}x}{2}+C$$

Equivalently, since $\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x-1$:

$$\frac{\tan^{2}x}{2}+C=\frac{\sec^{2}x}{2}+C'$$

**Check:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2}=\tan x\cdot\sec^{2}x$ ✓.

questions.question: Find a unit vector in the direction of vector $\left(\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
A unit vector along $\vec a$ is $\hat a=\dfrac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}$.

$$\left|\vec a\right|=\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt3$$

$$\therefore\ \hat a=\frac{\hat i+\hat j-\hat k}{\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat i+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat j-\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat k$$

**Check:** $\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{3}=1$ ✓ — the vector has unit length.

questions.question: Find the projection of the vector $\vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k$ on the vector $\vec b=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$.
questions.answer:
The projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$ is

$$\text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec b\right|}$$

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(2)(1)+(3)(2)+(2)(1)=2+6+2=10$$

$$\left|\vec b\right|=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt6$$

$$\therefore\ \text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{10}{\sqrt6}=\frac{10\sqrt6}{6}=\frac{5\sqrt6}{3}\approx4.082$$

**The projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$ is $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt6}=\dfrac{5\sqrt6}{3}$.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet computes $|\vec a|=\sqrt{17}$ and $|\vec b|=\sqrt6$, then quotes $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{17}}$ — but that is the projection of $\vec b$ on $\vec a$, not of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$. Dividing by the magnitude of the *target* vector is the rule, so the correct value is $\dfrac{10}{\sqrt6}$.

questions.question: If a line makes equal angles with the $x$, $y$ and $z$-axes, find its direction cosines.
questions.answer:
Let the line make angle $\theta$ with each of the three axes, so its direction cosines are

$$l=\cos\theta,\qquad m=\cos\theta,\qquad n=\cos\theta$$

Direction cosines always satisfy

$$l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$$

$$3\cos^{2}\theta=1\ \Rightarrow\ \cos^{2}\theta=\frac13\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\theta=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$$

$$\therefore\ (l,m,n)=\pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\ \frac{1}{\sqrt3},\ \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$$

**The direction cosines are $\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\ \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\ \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ with a common sign** (i.e. either all $+$ or all $-$), since the three cosines must be equal; this is the direction of the four body diagonals of a cube. Each angle is

$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\approx54.74^{\circ}$$

*(Note the constraint is 'equal angles', not merely 'equal magnitudes' — so only two of the eight sign combinations are admissible.)*

questions.question: If $f:R\to R$ be given by $f(x)=\left(7-x^{4}\right)^{1/4}$ then find the value of $f\circ f(x)$.
questions.answer:
(Here $f\circ f(x)$ means $f\left(f(x)\right)$.)

$$f(x)=\left(7-x^{4}\right)^{1/4}$$

$$f\left(f(x)\right)=\left[7-\left(f(x)\right)^{4}\right]^{1/4}$$

Now $\left(f(x)\right)^{4}=\left[\left(7-x^{4}\right)^{1/4}\right]^{4}=7-x^{4}$ (the fourth power undoes the fourth root), so

$$f\left(f(x)\right)=\left[7-\left(7-x^{4}\right)\right]^{1/4}$$

$$=\left[x^{4}\right]^{1/4}=x$$

$$\therefore\ f\circ f(x)=x$$

**This shows $f$ is its own inverse** ($f=f^{-1}$). Its domain is where $7-x^{4}\ge0$, i.e. $|x|\le\sqrt[4]{7}$, and on $[0,\sqrt[4]7]$ the value $(x^{4})^{1/4}=x$ (for negative $x$ the composition gives $|x|$).

questions.question: Prove that $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1+x}-\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{1+x}+\sqrt{1-x}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac12\cos^{-1}x$.
questions.answer:
**Put $x=\cos2\theta$**, so that $2\theta=\cos^{-1}x$ and $\theta=\dfrac12\cos^{-1}x$.

**Step 1 — simplify the numerator and denominator** using $1+\cos2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta$ and $1-\cos2\theta=2\sin^{2}\theta$:

$$\sqrt{1+x}=\sqrt{1+\cos2\theta}=\sqrt{2\cos^{2}\theta}=\sqrt2\cos\theta$$

$$\sqrt{1-x}=\sqrt{1-\cos2\theta}=\sqrt{2\sin^{2}\theta}=\sqrt2\sin\theta$$

**Step 2 — substitute into the L.H.S.:**

$$\text{L.H.S.}=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt2\cos\theta-\sqrt2\sin\theta}{\sqrt2\cos\theta+\sqrt2\sin\theta}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}\right)$$

**Step 3 — divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$:**

$$=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}\right)$$

**Step 4 — use the tangent subtraction formula** $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\theta\right)=\dfrac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\frac{\pi}{4}\tan\theta}=\dfrac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$ (since $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$):

$$=\tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta\right)\right]=\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta$$

**Step 5 — back-substitute $\theta=\dfrac12\cos^{-1}x$:**

$$\therefore\ \text{L.H.S.}=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12\cos^{-1}x=\text{R.H.S.}\qquad\blacksquare$$

*(Numerical check: at $x=0.2$ both sides are $0.10068$; at $x=0.6$ both are $0.32175$; at $x=-0.4$ both are $-0.20576$ ✓.)*

questions.question: Prove that $\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^{2}\\ x^{2}&1&x\\ x&x^{2}&1\end{vmatrix}=\left(1-x^{3}\right)^{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — column operation** $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$ (determinant unchanged):

$$D=\begin{vmatrix}1+x+x^{2}&x&x^{2}\\ 1+x+x^{2}&1&x\\ 1+x+x^{2}&x^{2}&1\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — take out the common factor** $(1+x+x^{2})$ from the first column:

$$D=\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^{2}\\ 1&1&x\\ 1&x^{2}&1\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — row operations** $R_2\to R_2-R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$:

$$D=\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^{2}\\ 0&1-x&x-x^{2}\\ 0&x^{2}-x&1-x^{2}\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 4 — expand along the first column:**

$$D=\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)\begin{vmatrix}1-x&x(1-x)\\ -x(1-x)&(1-x)(1+x)\end{vmatrix}$$

(using $x-x^{2}=x(1-x)$, $x^{2}-x=-x(1-x)$ and $1-x^{2}=(1-x)(1+x)$).

**Step 5 — take out $(1-x)$ from each row of the $2\times2$ determinant:**

$$\begin{vmatrix}1-x&x(1-x)\\ -x(1-x)&(1-x)(1+x)\end{vmatrix}=(1-x)^{2}\begin{vmatrix}1&x\\ -x&1+x\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=(1-x)^{2}\left[(1)(1+x)-x(-x)\right]=(1-x)^{2}\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)$$

**Step 6 — combine:**

$$D=\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)\cdot(1-x)^{2}\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)=(1-x)^{2}\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)^{2}$$

and since $(1-x)\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)=1-x^{3}$:

$$D=\left[(1-x)\left(1+x+x^{2}\right)\right]^{2}=\left(1-x^{3}\right)^{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^{2}\\ x^{2}&1&x\\ x&x^{2}&1\end{vmatrix}=\left(1-x^{3}\right)^{2}\qquad\blacksquare$$

*Check at $x=1$:* every entry of the matrix becomes $1$, so the determinant is $0$, and $(1-1^{3})^{2}=0$ ✓. *Check at $x=0$:* the determinant is $1$ and $(1-0)^{2}=1$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the value of $k$ so that the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$: $f(x)=\begin{cases}kx^{2}&,\ x\le2\\ 3&,\ x>2\end{cases}$
questions.answer:
Continuity at $x=2$ means

$$\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=f(2)$$

**Left-hand limit** (use $kx^{2}$, valid for $x\le2$):

$$\lim_{x\to2^{-}}kx^{2}=k(2)^{2}=4k$$

Also $f(2)=k(2)^{2}=4k$.

**Right-hand limit** (use the constant $3$, valid for $x>2$):

$$\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=3$$

**Equate:**

$$4k=3\ \Rightarrow\ k=\frac34$$

$$\therefore\ k=\frac{3}{4}$$

**Check:** with $k=\frac34$, the left piece is $\frac34x^{2}$, which gives $\frac34(4)=3$ at $x=2$ — matching the constant piece, so $f$ is continuous at $x=2$ ✓.

questions.question: If $e^{y}(x+1)=1$, show that $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — differentiate the given relation implicitly** with respect to $x$ (product rule on $e^{y}(x+1)$):

$$e^{y}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx}\cdot(x+1)+e^{y}\cdot1=0$$

Divide throughout by $e^{y}\ne0$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}(x+1)+1=0$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{x+1}\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Step 2 — differentiate again** with respect to $x$:

$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{d}{dx}\left[-(x+1)^{-1}\right]=-(-1)(x+1)^{-2}\cdot1$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 3 — compare.** From (1),

$$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{x+1}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}$$

which equals (2). Therefore

$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Sanity check from the explicit solution:** $e^{y}(x+1)=1$ gives $y=-\log(x+1)$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{x+1}$ and $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}$ — identical ✓.

questions.question: Or, if $(\cos x)^{y}=(\cos y)^{x}$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — take logarithms of both sides:**

$$\log\left[(\cos x)^{y}\right]=\log\left[(\cos y)^{x}\right]$$

$$y\log(\cos x)=x\log(\cos y)$$

**Step 2 — differentiate both sides implicitly.** Left side by the product rule, right side likewise:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}\log(\cos x)+y\cdot\frac{1}{\cos x}\cdot(-\sin x)=\log(\cos y)+x\cdot\frac{1}{\cos y}\cdot(-\sin y)\frac{dy}{dx}$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}\log(\cos x)-y\tan x=\log(\cos y)-x\tan y\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$

**Step 3 — collect the $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ terms:**

$$\frac{dy}{dx}\left[\log(\cos x)+x\tan y\right]=\log(\cos y)+y\tan x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\log(\cos y)+y\tan x}{\log(\cos x)+x\tan y}$$

**The derivative is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\log(\cos y)+y\tan x}{\log(\cos x)+x\tan y}$.**

*A neat check:* the relation $(\cos x)^{y}=(\cos y)^{x}$ is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, so the result must be symmetric too — and indeed the numerator is the denominator with $x\leftrightarrow y$ interchanged, so the answer equals the reciprocal of itself under the swap, as symmetry demands.

questions.question: Prove that $y=\dfrac{4\sin\theta}{2+\cos\theta}-\theta$ is an increasing function of $\theta$ in $[0,\pi/2]$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — differentiate** using the quotient rule on the first term:

$$\frac{dy}{d\theta}=\frac{4\cos\theta\,(2+\cos\theta)-4\sin\theta\,(-\sin\theta)}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}-1$$

$$=\frac{8\cos\theta+4\cos^{2}\theta+4\sin^{2}\theta}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}-1$$

Since $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$:

$$\frac{dy}{d\theta}=\frac{8\cos\theta+4}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}-1$$

**Step 2 — put over a common denominator:**

$$\frac{dy}{d\theta}=\frac{8\cos\theta+4-(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}$$

$$=\frac{8\cos\theta+4-\left(4+4\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta\right)}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}$$

$$=\frac{4\cos\theta-\cos^{2}\theta}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}=\frac{\cos\theta\,(4-\cos\theta)}{(2+\cos\theta)^{2}}$$

**Step 3 — sign on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.** There $\cos\theta\ge0$ and $\cos\theta\le1<4$, so

$$\cos\theta\,(4-\cos\theta)\ge0,\qquad (2+\cos\theta)^{2}>0$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{d\theta}\ge0\ \text{throughout}\ \left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$$

Hence $y$ is an **increasing function** of $\theta$ on $\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ ✓

**Values to illustrate:** $y(0)=0$; $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{4/\sqrt2}{2+1/\sqrt2}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\approx1.094-0.785=0.309$; $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=4-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\approx2.429$ — steadily rising ✓

*Note on the printed question:* the booklet's question line prints the denominator as $3+\cos\theta$, while its own answer starts from $y=\dfrac{4\sin\theta}{2+\cos\theta}-\theta$. The denominator **must be $2$**: with $3+\cos\theta$ the derivative works out to $\dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta+6\cos\theta-6}{(3+\cos\theta)^{2}}$, which equals $-\dfrac59$ at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and is therefore *not* increasing on the interval. The statement is true for the denominator $2$, and that is the version proved above.

questions.question: Or, a balloon, which always remains spherical, has a variable radius. Find the rate at which its volume is increasing with respect to the radius when the radius is 10 cm.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — volume as a function of radius:**

$$V=\frac43\pi r^{3}$$

**Step 2 — differentiate with respect to $r$:**

$$\frac{dV}{dr}=\frac43\pi\cdot3r^{2}=4\pi r^{2}$$

**Step 3 — evaluate at $r=10$ cm:**

$$\left.\frac{dV}{dr}\right|_{r=10}=4\pi(10)^{2}=400\pi\ \text{cm}^{3}/\text{cm}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dV}{dr}=400\pi\approx1256.6\ \text{cm}^{3}\ \text{per cm}$$

**The volume is increasing at $400\pi$ cm³ per cm** of radius.

**Geometric reading:** $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=4\pi r^{2}$ is exactly the **surface area** of the sphere — the rate of change of volume with radius equals the area of the shell added, which is the natural interpretation of a derivative as 'shell volume per unit thickness'. Note that no information about *time* is needed, because the question asks for the rate *with respect to the radius*.

questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — write the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic plus a constant.**

Let

$$x+2=A\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}+2x+3\right)+B=A(2x+2)+B$$

Comparing coefficients of $x$: $1=2A$, so $A=\dfrac12$.

Comparing constants: $2=2A+B=1+B$, so $B=1$.

$$\therefore\ x+2=\frac12(2x+2)+1$$

**Step 2 — split the integral:**

$$I=\frac12\int\frac{(2x+2)\,dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}+\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}$$

**Step 3 — the first part** by substituting $t=x^{2}+2x+3$, $dt=(2x+2)\,dx$:

$$\frac12\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt t}=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt t=\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}$$

**Step 4 — the second part** by completing the square, $x^{2}+2x+3=(x+1)^{2}+2=(x+1)^{2}+\left(\sqrt2\right)^{2}$:

$$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}+2}}=\log\left|(x+1)+\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}\right|$$

(using $\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^{2}+a^{2}}}=\log\left|u+\sqrt{u^{2}+a^{2}}\right|$ with $u=x+1$, $a=\sqrt2$).

**Step 5 — combine:**

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}dx=\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}+\log\left|x+1+\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}\right|+C$$

**Check:** differentiating the first term gives $\dfrac{2x+2}{2\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}=\dfrac{x+1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}$, and the second gives $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}$; their sum is $\dfrac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}$ ✓

questions.topic: Partial Fractions with a Repeated Factor
questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{(x-1)^{2}(x+2)}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — partial fractions.** The repeated factor $(x-1)^{2}$ needs two terms:

$$\frac{x}{(x-1)^{2}(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^{2}}+\frac{C}{x+2}$$

Multiplying by $(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$:

$$x=A(x-1)(x+2)+B(x+2)+C(x-1)^{2}$$

**Put $x=1$:** $1=B(3)$, so $B=\dfrac13$.

**Put $x=-2$:** $-2=C(-3)^{2}=9C$, so $C=-\dfrac29$.

**Put $x=0$:** $0=A(-1)(2)+B(2)+C(1)=-2A+\dfrac23-\dfrac29$, so $-2A=\dfrac29-\dfrac23=-\dfrac49$ and $A=\dfrac29$.

(Check the $x^{2}$ coefficient: $A+C=\dfrac29-\dfrac29=0$ ✓, as it must be since the left side has no $x^{2}$ term.)

**Step 2 — integrate term by term:**

$$I=\frac29\int\frac{dx}{x-1}+\frac13\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^{2}}-\frac29\int\frac{dx}{x+2}$$

$$=\frac29\log|x-1|+\frac13\cdot\frac{(x-1)^{-1}}{-1}-\frac29\log|x+2|+C$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac{2}{9}\log\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right|-\frac{1}{3(x-1)}+C$$

$$=\frac{2}{9}\log|x-1|-\frac{1}{3(x-1)}-\frac{2}{9}\log|x+2|+C$$

**Check** by differentiating: $\dfrac{2}{9(x-1)}+\dfrac{1}{3(x-1)^{2}}-\dfrac{2}{9(x+2)}$, which combines to $\dfrac{x}{(x-1)^{2}(x+2)}$ ✓

questions.question: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{3}x+\cos^{3}x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let

$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{3}x+\cos^{3}x}dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$

Use $\displaystyle\int_0^{a}f(x)dx=\int_0^{a}f(a-x)dx$ with $a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; since $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\sin x$,

$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^{3}x}{\cos^{3}x+\sin^{3}x}dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Add (1) and (2):** the integrands have the same denominator, and the numerators add to the denominator itself:

$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^{3}x+\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{3}x+\cos^{3}x}dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx$$

$$2I=\left[x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{3}x}{\sin^{3}x+\cos^{3}x}dx=\frac{\pi}{4}\approx0.7854$$

*(The same trick works with any common power: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{n}x}{\sin^{n}x+\cos^{n}x}dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$ for every $n$. $I$ is exactly half of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ because the two forms of $I$ are complementary halves of the integral of $1$.)*

questions.topic: Angle Between Sides of a Triangle
questions.question: If the vertices A, B and C of a triangle ABC are $(1,2,3)$, $(-1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,2)$ respectively, then find $\angle ABC$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the two vectors that meet at $B$:**

$$\vec{BA}=\vec{OA}-\vec{OB}=\left(\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k\right)-\left(-\hat i\right)=2\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$$

$$\vec{BC}=\vec{OC}-\vec{OB}=\left(\hat j+2\hat k\right)-\left(-\hat i\right)=\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$$

**Step 2 — magnitudes and dot product:**

$$\left|\vec{BA}\right|=\sqrt{4+4+9}=\sqrt{17}$$

$$\left|\vec{BC}\right|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$$

$$\vec{BA}\cdot\vec{BC}=(2)(1)+(2)(1)+(3)(2)=2+2+6=10$$

**Step 3 — the angle:**

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec{BA}\cdot\vec{BC}}{\left|\vec{BA}\right|\left|\vec{BC}\right|}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt6}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{102}}$$

$$\therefore\ \angle ABC=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\right)$$

$$\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\right)=\cos^{-1}(0.99015)\approx8.05^{\circ}$$

**So $\angle ABC=\cos^{-1}\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{102}}\approx8.05^{\circ}$** — a very sharp angle at $B$, which is consistent with the triangle's sketch where $B$ is the acute corner.

questions.question: Find the angle between the following pair of lines: $\vec r=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k+\lambda\left(\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=2\hat i-\hat j-5\hat k+\mu\left(3\hat i-5\hat j-4\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors:

$$\vec b_1=\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k,\qquad \vec b_2=3\hat i-5\hat j-4\hat k$$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2}{\left|\vec b_1\right|\left|\vec b_2\right|}$$

**Dot product:**

$$\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=(1)(3)+(-1)(-5)+(-2)(-4)=3+5+8=16$$

**Magnitudes:**

$$\left|\vec b_1\right|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$$

$$\left|\vec b_2\right|=\sqrt{9+25+16}=\sqrt{50}$$

**Therefore:**

$$\cos\theta=\frac{16}{\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt{50}}=\frac{16}{\sqrt{300}}=\frac{16}{10\sqrt3}=\frac{8}{5\sqrt3}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{5\sqrt3}\right)=\cos^{-1}(0.92376)\approx22.6^{\circ}$$

**The angle between the lines is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{8}{5\sqrt3}\approx22.6^{\circ}$** (and since $\cos\theta>0$, this is already the acute angle).

questions.question: If a coin is tossed three times, find $P(E/F)$, where $E\to$ at least two heads, $F\to$ at most one head.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the sample space** (8 equally likely ordered outcomes):

$$S=\{HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ THH,\ HTT,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT\},\qquad n(S)=8$$

**Step 2 — the two events:**

$$E=\{\text{at least two heads}\}=\{HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ THH\},\qquad n(E)=4$$

$$F=\{\text{at most one head}\}=\{HTT,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT\},\qquad n(F)=4$$

**Step 3 — the intersection.** $E$ contains only outcomes with two or three heads; $F$ contains only outcomes with zero or one head. No outcome can be in both:

$$E\cap F=\varnothing,\qquad n(E\cap F)=0$$

**Step 4 — conditional probability:**

$$P\left(\frac{E}{F}\right)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}=\frac{0}{4/8}=0$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E}{F}\right)=0$$

**The events are mutually exclusive**, so the answer is **0** — given that there is at most one head, it is impossible that there are at least two.

*Note on the printed key:* the arithmetic $\frac{0}{3}=0$ is right, but the booklet's listing of $F$ omits the outcome $TTT$ (giving $n(F)=3$). With $TTT$ included, $n(F)=4$; the answer remains $0$ because the numerator is $0$.

questions.topic: System of Equations by Matrix Method
questions.question: Solve the system of linear equations using matrix method: $x-y+2z=7$, $3x+4y-5z=-5$, $2x-y+3z=12$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — write as $AX=B$:**

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&2\\ 3&4&-5\\ 2&-1&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{bmatrix}7\\-5\\12\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — determinant** (expand along the first row):

$$|A|=1\begin{vmatrix}4&-5\\-1&3\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}3&-5\\2&3\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}3&4\\2&-1\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=1(12-5)+1(9+10)+2(-3-8)$$

$$=7+19-22=4\ne0$$

So $A^{-1}$ exists and the solution is unique: $X=A^{-1}B$.

**Step 3 — cofactors** (sign pattern $\begin{smallmatrix}+&-&+\\-&+&-\\+&-&+\end{smallmatrix}$):

$$C_{11}=12-5=7,\quad C_{12}=-(9+10)=-19,\quad C_{13}=-3-8=-11$$

$$C_{21}=-\left(-3-(-2)\right)=1,\quad C_{22}=3-4=-1,\quad C_{23}=-\left(-1-(-2)\right)=-1$$

$$C_{31}=5-8=-3,\quad C_{32}=-\left(-5-6\right)=11,\quad C_{33}=4-(-3)=7$$

$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}7&1&-3\\-19&-1&11\\-11&-1&7\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 4 — the solution:**

$$X=\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}7&1&-3\\-19&-1&11\\-11&-1&7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7\\-5\\12\end{bmatrix}$$

Row 1: $49-5-36=8$

Row 2: $-133+5+132=4$

Row 3: $-77+5+84=12$

$$X=\frac14\begin{bmatrix}8\\4\\12\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\3\end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore\ x=2,\quad y=1,\quad z=3$$

**Check:** $2-1+6=7$ ✓; $6+4-15=-5$ ✓; $4-1+9=12$ ✓.

questions.question: Or, obtain the inverse of the matrix using elementary operations: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&3&2\\ 3&0&4\\ 2&5&0\end{bmatrix}$.
Find the maximum and minimum value of given function: $f(x)=41-72x-18x^{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**

$$f'(x)=-72-36x$$

Set $f'(x)=0$:

$$-72-36x=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=-2$$

**Step 2 — second derivative test:**

$$f''(x)=-36<0$$

Since the second derivative is negative everywhere, $f$ is **concave down** and $x=-2$ is a point of **maximum**.

**Step 3 — the value:**

$$f(-2)=41-72(-2)-18(-2)^{2}$$

$$=41+144-18(4)=41+144-72=113$$

$$\therefore\ f_{\max}=113\ \text{at}\ x=-2$$

The curve is a downward parabola with vertex $(-2,113)$, so

$$f(x)\le113\ \text{for all real }x$$

**Minimum:** since $-18x^{2}\to-\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, the function has **no minimum value** on $\mathbb{R}$ — it decreases without bound.

**So the maximum value is $113$ (at $x=-2$), and there is no minimum value.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet computes $x=-2$, $f''(-2)=-36<0$ and $f(-2)=113$ correctly, calling it the maximum. It does not state that no minimum exists; on the whole real line this parabola is unbounded below.

questions.topic: Area Between a Circle and a Parabola
questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the circle $4x^{2}+4y^{2}=9$ and the parabola $x^{2}=4y$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — describe the curves.**

$$4x^{2}+4y^{2}=9\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac94=\left(\frac32\right)^{2}$$

so it is a circle with centre $(0,0)$ and radius $\dfrac32$.

The parabola $x^{2}=4y$ opens upward with vertex at the origin.

**Step 2 — find the points of intersection** by substituting $x^{2}=4y$ into the circle:

$$4(4y)+4y^{2}=9\ \Rightarrow\ 4y^{2}+16y-9=0$$

$$4y^{2}+18y-2y-9=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2y(2y+9)-(2y+9)=0$$

$$(2y-1)(2y+9)=0$$

$$y=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad y=-\frac92$$

For $y=\dfrac12$: $x^{2}=4\left(\dfrac12\right)=2$, so $x=\pm\sqrt2$ ✓ (on the circle).

For $y=-\dfrac92$: $x^{2}=4\left(-\dfrac92\right)=-18<0$, which gives no real $x$ — reject.

$$\therefore\ \text{the curves meet at}\ \left(\sqrt2,\ \frac12\right)\ \text{and}\ \left(-\sqrt2,\ \frac12\right)$$

**Step 3 — set up the area.** Between $x=-\sqrt2$ and $x=\sqrt2$, the circle lies above the parabola ($\frac32=1.5$ at $x=0$ versus $0$). So

$$A=\int_{-\sqrt2}^{\sqrt2}\left(y_{\text{circle}}-y_{\text{parabola}}\right)dx=\int_{-\sqrt2}^{\sqrt2}\left(\sqrt{\frac94-x^{2}}-\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)dx$$

By symmetry about the $y$-axis,

$$A=2\int_0^{\sqrt2}\left(\sqrt{\frac94-x^{2}}-\frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)dx$$

**Step 4 — integrate.**

$$\int\sqrt{\frac94-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{\frac94-x^{2}}+\frac{9}{8}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)$$

$$\int\frac{x^{2}}{4}dx=\frac{x^{3}}{12}$$

So (for the symmetric half)

$$\frac{A}{2}=\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{\frac94-x^{2}}+\frac98\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{x^{3}}{12}\right]_0^{\sqrt2}$$

At $x=\sqrt2$: $\sqrt{\frac94-2}=\sqrt{\frac14}=\frac12$, so the first term is $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12=\frac{\sqrt2}{4}$; the second is $\frac98\sin^{-1}\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$; the third is $\frac{2\sqrt2}{12}=\frac{\sqrt2}{6}$.

At $x=0$: all three terms vanish.

$$\frac{A}{2}=\frac{\sqrt2}{4}-\frac{\sqrt2}{6}+\frac98\sin^{-1}\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}=\frac{3\sqrt2-2\sqrt2}{12}+\frac98\sin^{-1}\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$$

$$\therefore\ A=2\left[\frac{\sqrt2}{12}+\frac98\sin^{-1}\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right]=\frac{\sqrt2}{6}+\frac94\sin^{-1}\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$$

$$A\approx0.2357+2.7697=3.0054\ \text{sq. units}$$

**The area of the region is $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{6}+\dfrac94\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\approx3.005$ square units.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet integrates only $\int_0^{\sqrt2}4x\,dx$ — that is, the area under the *line* $4x$, not under the circle — and obtains $\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$. The intersection points it finds, $\left(\pm\sqrt2,\frac12\right)$, are right, but the area expression is not the area between the two curves. The correct area is the one derived above (numerically verified: $3.00536$).

questions.question: Find particular solution of the differential equation: $2xy-y^{2}-2x^{2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, $y=2$ when $x=1$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — solve for the derivative:**

$$2x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy-y^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2xy-y^{2}}{2x^{2}}$$

The right-hand side is homogeneous of degree $0$, so put $y=vx$, giving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:

$$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2x(vx)-v^{2}x^{2}}{2x^{2}}=\frac{2v-v^{2}}{2}$$

**Step 2 — separate:**

$$x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2v-v^{2}}{2}-v=\frac{2v-v^{2}-2v}{2}=-\frac{v^{2}}{2}$$

$$-2\frac{dv}{v^{2}}=\frac{dx}{x}$$

**Step 3 — integrate:**

$$-2\int v^{-2}dv=\int\frac{dx}{x}$$

$$-2\left(-\frac1v\right)=\log x+C\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{2}{v}=\log x+C$$

**Step 4 — back-substitute $v=\dfrac yx$:**

$$\frac{2x}{y}=\log x+C\ \Rightarrow\ 2x=y\left(\log x+C\right)$$

**Step 5 — apply $y=2$ at $x=1$** (note $\log1=0$):

$$2(1)=2\left(0+C\right)\ \Rightarrow\ 2=2C\ \Rightarrow\ C=1$$

**Step 6 — the particular solution:**

$$\therefore\ 2x=y\left(1+\log x\right)\ \ \text{i.e.}\ \ y=\frac{2x}{1+\log x}$$

**Check:** at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac{2}{1+0}=2$ ✓. And differentiating $y(1+\log x)=2x$ implicitly gives $y'\left(1+\log x\right)+y\cdot\dfrac1x=2$, i.e. $y'\left(1+\log x\right)+\dfrac yx=2$; multiplying by $\dfrac{yx}{2}$-type combinations reproduces $2xy-y^{2}=2x^{2}y'$ ✓.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet ends at $2x=y\log x+Cy$ with $C=1$, i.e. $2x=y\log x+y$, which is the same relation $2x=y(1+\log x)$ ✓ — correct.

questions.question: Or, find the general solution of the differential equation: $\cos^{2}x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=\tan x$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — put the equation in standard linear form** by dividing by $\cos^{2}x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{\cos^{2}x}=\frac{\tan x}{\cos^{2}x}$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}+y\sec^{2}x=\tan x\sec^{2}x\qquad\ldots(1)$$

This is linear, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ with

$$P=\sec^{2}x,\qquad Q=\tan x\sec^{2}x$$

**Step 2 — the integrating factor:**

$$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\int\sec^{2}x\,dx}=e^{\tan x}$$

**Step 3 — multiply (1) throughout by the I.F.** (the left side becomes the derivative of $y\cdot$I.F.):

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\,e^{\tan x}\right)=e^{\tan x}\tan x\sec^{2}x$$

$$y\,e^{\tan x}=\int e^{\tan x}\tan x\sec^{2}x\,dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 4 — evaluate the integral.** Put $z=\tan x$, so $dz=\sec^{2}x\,dx$:

$$\int z\,e^{z}dz$$

Integrate by parts with $u=z$, $dv=e^{z}dz$ (so $du=dz$, $v=e^{z}$):

$$\int z\,e^{z}dz=z\,e^{z}-\int e^{z}dz=z\,e^{z}-e^{z}=e^{z}(z-1)$$

$$\therefore\ \int e^{\tan x}\tan x\sec^{2}x\,dx=e^{\tan x}\left(\tan x-1\right)$$

**Step 5 — back to (2):**

$$y\,e^{\tan x}=e^{\tan x}\left(\tan x-1\right)+C$$

**Step 6 — divide by $e^{\tan x}$:**

$$\therefore\ y=\tan x-1+C\,e^{-\tan x}$$

**Check:** differentiating, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sec^{2}x-C e^{-\tan x}\sec^{2}x$, so

$$\cos^{2}x\frac{dy}{dx}+y=1-C e^{-\tan x}+\tan x-1+Ce^{-\tan x}=\tan x\ ✓$$

**The general solution is $y=\tan x-1+Ce^{-\tan x}$.**

questions.question: Find the shortest distance between the lines $\vec r=6\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k+\lambda\left(\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=-4\hat i-\hat k+\mu\left(3\hat i-2\hat j-2\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — identify the data.**

$$\vec a_1=6\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k,\qquad \vec b_1=\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k$$

$$\vec a_2=-4\hat i+0\hat j-\hat k,\qquad \vec b_2=3\hat i-2\hat j-2\hat k$$

The direction vectors are **not** parallel, so the lines are skew (or intersecting); for skew lines

$$d=\frac{\left|\left(\vec a_2-\vec a_1\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|}$$

**Step 2 — the vector between the two points:**

$$\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(-4-6)\hat i+(0-2)\hat j+(-1-2)\hat k=-10\hat i-2\hat j-3\hat k$$

**Step 3 — the cross product:**

$$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 1&-2&2\\ 3&-2&-2\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-2)(-2)-(2)(-2)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(-2)-(2)(3)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(-2)-(-2)(3)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(4+4)-\hat j(-2-6)+\hat k(-2+6)=8\hat i+8\hat j+4\hat k$$

$$\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|=\sqrt{64+64+16}=\sqrt{144}=12$$

**Step 4 — the dot product:**

$$\left(-10\hat i-2\hat j-3\hat k\right)\cdot\left(8\hat i+8\hat j+4\hat k\right)=-80-16-12=-108$$

**Step 5 — the distance:**

$$d=\frac{\left|-108\right|}{12}=\frac{108}{12}=9$$

$$\therefore\ \text{shortest distance}=9\ \text{units}$$

**The shortest distance between the two lines is 9 units.** (The value is non-zero, confirming the lines are skew rather than intersecting.)

questions.question: A card from a pack of 52 cards is lost. From the remaining cards of the pack, two cards are drawn and are found to be both diamond. Find the probability of the lost card being a diamond.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — define the events.**

$$E_1=\{\text{the lost card is a diamond}\},\qquad E_2=\{\text{the lost card is not a diamond}\}$$

$$P(E_1)=\frac{13}{52}=\frac14,\qquad P(E_2)=\frac{39}{52}=\frac34$$

Let $E$ = 'the two cards drawn from the remaining 51 are both diamonds'.

**Step 2 — the conditional probabilities.**

If a diamond is lost, $12$ diamonds remain among $51$ cards:

$$P(E/E_1)=\frac{12}{51}\cdot\frac{11}{50}=\frac{132}{2550}$$

If a non-diamond is lost, all $13$ diamonds remain among $51$ cards:

$$P(E/E_2)=\frac{13}{51}\cdot\frac{12}{50}=\frac{156}{2550}$$

**Step 3 — Bayes' theorem:**

$$P(E_1/E)=\frac{P(E_1)P(E/E_1)}{P(E_1)P(E/E_1)+P(E_2)P(E/E_2)}$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $4\times2550$ to clear fractions:

$$P(E_1/E)=\frac{1\times132}{1\times132+3\times156}=\frac{132}{132+468}=\frac{132}{600}$$

$$\therefore\ P(E_1/E)=\frac{132}{600}=\frac{11}{50}=0.22$$

**The probability that the lost card is a diamond is $\dfrac{11}{50}=0.22$.**

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's 'solution' is a copy of an unrelated urn problem — it defines $E_1,E_2,E_3$ as 'the balls are drawn from urn A, urn B, urn C', mentions 'one white and red', and computes ${}^{1}C_1\times{}^{3}C_1/{}^{6}C_2$ etc. None of that belongs to this card question, so the printed answer cannot be used. The correct working is the Bayes calculation above, giving $\dfrac{11}{50}$.

questions.question: Minimise $Z=x+2y$ subject to $2x+y\ge3$, $x+2y\ge6$ and $x,y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — convert to lines.**

**Line 1:** $2x+y=3$. Intercepts: $\left(\dfrac32,0\right)$ and $(0,3)$. The origin gives $0\ge3$, false, so the feasible half-plane is the one **away from** the origin.

**Line 2:** $x+2y=6$. Intercepts: $(6,0)$ and $(0,3)$. The origin gives $0\ge6$, false, again the half-plane **away from** the origin.

**Step 2 — the feasible region.** Both lines pass through $(0,3)$, so the region is the **unbounded** wedge bounded by the two lines above and to the right, with corner points

$$A(0,3),\qquad B(6,0)$$

(and extending to infinity in the direction of increasing $x$ and $y$).

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=x+2y$ at the corners:**

$$Z(0,3)=0+2(3)=6$$

$$Z(6,0)=6+2(0)=6$$

**Step 4 — conclusion.** Both corners give $Z=6$, and since $Z=x+2y$ grows along any unbounded direction of the region, $6$ is the smallest value. It is attained along the whole segment joining $(0,3)$ and $(6,0)$:

$$\therefore\ Z_{\min}=6\ \text{at every point of the segment joining}\ (0,3)\ \text{and}\ (6,0)$$

*(Sanity check: the segment joining $(0,3)$ to $(6,0)$ is $x+2y=6$, on which $Z=x+2y=6$ identically — hence the minimum is attained on a whole edge, not just at a vertex. This is the 'alternative optimum' case.)*

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet lists the corner points as $(0,3)$ and $(6,0)$, gets $Z=6$ at both, and concludes 'minimum $z=6$ at all points on the line segment joining the points $(6,0)$ and $(0,3)$' — which is correct.
